sections.h2: Which office to call about real estate taxes
sections.html:
Start with the Summit County Fiscal Office, which houses Auditor, Treasurer and Recorder divisions under a single elected Fiscal Officer. The Auditor division sets values and rates, the Treasurer division issues bills and takes money, and a Board of Revision hears value disputes. County charter creates this one-office setup, and the Fiscal Officer does the work other counties spread across a separate auditor, treasurer and recorder.

The Ohio Building at 175 S. Main St. in Akron is under renovation, which pushed the divisions into temporary quarters, so phone first:

  • Main office: 1-888-388-5613
  • Treasurer: 330-643-2588
  • Real Estate and Appraisal, which handles homestead and assessments: 330-643-2710
  • Board of Revision: 330-926-2559 or bor@summitoh.net
  • Delinquent Tax Department: 330-643-2600

About 538,000 people live in the county, in homes that are mostly owner-occupied (67.5 percent). The median value of those homes is $208,700, renters pay a median $1,026, and median household income is $71,622. Those medians cover the whole county, so any one street may differ. Akron is the seat and largest city.

Seventy-four taxing authorities share the bill: the county, 5 county agencies, 26 school districts, 8 library districts, 14 cities, 8 villages, 9 townships, a water district, a fire district and a recreation district. The two leading digits of a parcel number identify your taxing district, and that district decides the rate.

sections.h2: What goes into a tax bill
sections.html:
Ohio taxes 35 percent of appraised value. The rate stacks up levies that local voters approved. The Fiscal Officer has no power to raise or lower taxes, and the tax rates page links three years of effective rate summaries. Levies come in five kinds:

  • Additional: new money for a taxing body, so bills rise.
  • Renewal: the same yield as an expiring levy.
  • Replacement: swaps in current values for a levy built on old ones, so bills move with the market.
  • Emergency: schools only, a fixed yearly sum over a stated span.
  • Bond: covers principal and interest on a permanent improvement.

The summary of charges on a bill shows the reduction factor, non-business credit, owner-occupancy credit, homestead reduction, current net taxes and current assessments. A bill covers the year before, because Ohio collects one year in arrears. Akron residents with an assessment question call 330-375-2484, and everyone else calls 330-643-2645.

sections.h2: How late can I pay, and what does a miss cost?
sections.html:
Dates print on the bill. There is no grace period, and never receiving a bill is no defense. A missed first half draws a 10 percent penalty. Miss the second half too and the full unpaid current balance, first-half amount included, takes another 10 percent. Under R.C. 323.121(C), paying everything within ten days after a deadline halves that penalty.

Ways to pay:

  • A counter visit to the Treasurer division, checks payable to the Fiscal Officer or Fiscal Office.
  • Mail with a U.S. postmark on or before the deadline. Private meter stamps are rejected.
  • A bank listed on your bill, available only while a collection is open.
  • Phone or web through Official Payments Corporation, which charges 1 percent on debit (minimum $3.95), 2.75 percent on credit (minimum $3.95) or $1.00 per electronic check.
  • Cash at a MoneyGram location, plus a service fee.

Summit also runs a prepayment plan, the Real Estate Discount program. Owners with no delinquency sign up between July 1 and October 31 for a first half, or between January 1 and March 31 for a second half, pay on five of six coupons and earn credit on the early money. Missing the last coupon forfeits the credit.

Use the Board of Revision, whose window runs from the first of January through the end of March. It rules on value alone and never on the tax amount, and the owner has to prove the claim with paperwork.

Summit County Board of Revision complaints
StepWhat to know
WindowJanuary 1 to March 31
DeliveryMail postmarked by the deadline, a counter visit, or Smartfile online
SeatsFiscal Officer, County Executive, Clerk of Courts, or designees
ProofHanded in, mailed, or uploaded with an online filing
Legal weightFiling starts a legal proceeding

Values are redone every six years, with an update in year three, by comparing a parcel with neighborhood sales. Permits tip off the office to new building. Rewiring, replumbing, framing or foundation work can raise value, while a new roof or routine remodeling does not.

With a complaint pending, R.C. 5715.19 allows you to tender tax computed on your claimed value, with interest on any shortfall if the final number lands higher. Evidence withheld from the board can be excluded on appeal. For storm, fire, flood or demolition damage, file DTE Form 26 by December 31 (damage in the year's first nine months) or by January 31 (last three months).

The homestead exemption removes the first $29,000 of appraised value on a single-family home from tax, and the office puts average savings at $535 yearly. It covers owners 65 by December 31, the permanently and totally disabled, owners who are rated 100 percent disabled by a service-connected injury, and spouses of first responders who died on duty. The service-connected group sees $58,000 exempted. The 2026 income ceiling for age and disability claims is $41,000, using the owner's and spouse's Ohio adjusted gross income.

The owner-occupancy reduction needs you to own and live in the home on January 1, with the application in by December 31. Rentals are out. It ends when the property transfers, so an incoming owner-occupant files again.

At transfer, R.C. 319.202 has the buyer's conveyance statement confirm that the seller was asked about these reductions. If the house gets one, a sworn note estimating the amount travels with it. Your title company will request the answer.

sections.h2: Back taxes on a Summit County house
sections.html:
The Delinquent Tax Payment Plan, started in 1987, takes owners who missed a half and sets monthly installments. The old balance freezes in a special account with no added interest, leftover interest is abated at completion, and new bills must be paid on time.

The office sells tax certificate liens each late October. Paying in full or entering a plan keeps a lien off that sale. If you would rather sell, ask the title company to request a payoff figure from the Treasurer division and settle it at closing.

Closing is the practical deadline. A buyer's lender will not fund over an open delinquency, so the payoff comes out of your proceeds. Call the Delinquent Tax Department at 330-643-2600 early, before the listing, so you know the number and whether a plan is in place that the buyer must be told about.

faqs.q: What is the late fee on Summit County property tax?
faqs.a: It is 10 percent of the unpaid half. Full payment within ten days after the deadline gets half of that penalty waived under state law.

faqs.q: Can I use the Real Estate Discount program while I owe back taxes?
faqs.a: No. Taxes must be current to enroll. Owners who are behind should ask about the Delinquent Tax Payment Plan.

faqs.q: How soon must I report fire or storm damage to the Fiscal Office?
faqs.a: File DTE Form 26 by December 31 for damage from January through September, or by January 31 of the following year for October through December damage. Send it to appraisedvalue@summitoh.net or mail it in.
The Fiscal Office property search finds it from a name, address or the number itself. Its first two digits name the taxing district.

faqs.q: Does a postmark on the due date count?
faqs.a: A Postal Service postmark on the due date counts, while a private meter mark does not. Under state law the earliest postmark on the envelope sets the payment date.
